title: ～た
summary: た on the end of a verb puts it in the past, the way friends say it: 来る (come), 来た (came).
parts: ついに来た！
I'm finally here!
Verbs like 食べる just swap る for た: 食べた. 来る is one of two verbs that change their own way: 来る, 来た (くる, きた).
more: お腹すいた。
I'm hungry. (My stomach has emptied.)
Other verbs change their last sound before た: すく, すいた; 買う, 買った; 飲む, 飲んだ.
This plain form is what you use with friends. The polite past is ～ました: 来ました.

A verb's last sound decides between た and だ. いる, 食べる and most verbs ending -iru or -eru are "る verbs": they drop る (食べた). For the rest, う, つ and る become ～った (買った, 待った, わかった); む, ぶ and ぬ become ～んだ (飲んだ, 呼んだ); く becomes ～いた (書いた), ぐ becomes ～いだ; す becomes ～した (話した). 行く is the odd one: 行った. する is した, and 来る is 来た (きた).
An i-adjective changes too: うまい, うまかった; 高い, 高かった. いい becomes よかった.

title: だ / です
summary: だ ends a sentence that says what something is: 成田だ, it's Narita. Friends say だ or leave it off; strangers and staff say です.
parts: 成田だ。
It's Narita.
だ comes at the very end of the sentence. In casual talk it's often left off, especially in questions.
いい部屋だ！
It's a nice room!
です means the same thing, politely. You'll hear it from staff and strangers.
more: きれいな部屋だ！
It's a beautiful room!
Before a noun, だ becomes な. Words like きれい that work this way are called na-adjectives.
だ never follows an i-adjective (高い, 多い): say 高い。 or 高いよ, not 高いだ.
Past: 朝までゲームだった, I was gaming till morning.

title: が
summary: が points at who or what does something, or what a description is about: 人が多い, there are lots of people.
parts: 人が多い。
There are a lot of people.
は sets the topic for what follows; が picks out the one thing the sentence is about. A question word always takes が: 誰が来た？
ビルが高い。
The buildings are tall.
more: が is also for what you've just noticed (雨が降ってる！), and for what you like, understand or have (ラーメンが好き). は sets one thing against others: コーヒーは飲まない, coffee I don't drink.

title: は
summary: は marks what you're talking about. It's written は but said "wa". On its own with a rising voice, it asks "what about…?"
parts: 駅は？
Where's the station? (What about the station?)
The topic comes first, then は, then what you say about it.
駅は、あっちだ。
The station's that way.

title: ～ない
summary: ない on a verb makes it negative, the way friends say it: わかる (understand), わからない (don't understand).
parts: わからない。
I don't know.
いる, 食べる and most verbs ending -iru or -eru are "る verbs": drop る. The rest move their last sound to the "a" row: わかる, わからない; 言う, 言わない.
人は多くない。
It's not crowded.
An i-adjective changes too: 多い, 多くない.
more: する and 来る change their own way: しない, 来ない (こない).
いない。
Nobody's here.
A final う becomes わ, not あ: 言う, 言わない; 買う, 買わない. ある has no ない form of its own: its negative is just ない.
An i-adjective swaps its い for くない: 多い, 多くない; 高い, 高くない. いい becomes よくない.

title: よ / ね / な / でしょ
summary: よ at the end tells someone something they don't know yet. ね looks for agreement, like "right?" or "huh". な is said half to yourself. でしょ? is surer: "told you".
parts: ユキだよ。
I'm Yuki.
よ is friendly emphasis: you're filling the listener in.
いい部屋だね。
It's a nice room, huh.
ね assumes the listener sees it the same way.
more: 大きいな。
It's big, huh.
な is ね said to yourself: a thought out loud, not a question for anyone.
大きいでしょ？
Big, right?
でしょ? expects a yes: you knew it, and you're checking they see it too. Said flat, でしょう is a polite guess, "probably".

title: の
summary: の joins two nouns, like 's or "of": アレックスの部屋, Alex's room.
parts: アレックスの部屋。
Alex's room.
The first noun owns or describes the second.
ここのラーメン。
The ramen here.

title: ～たい
summary: たい on a verb's stem means you want to do it: 食べる, 食べたい, want to eat.
parts: ラーメン、食べたい？
Want some ramen?
Drop る from a る verb, or move other verbs to their "i" sound, and add たい: やる, やりたい.
It changes like an adjective: 食べたくない is "don't want to eat".

title: を
summary: を marks what a verb is done to: ラーメンを食べる, eat ramen. It's said "o".
parts: ラーメンを食べる。
I eat ramen.
Friends often drop it: ラーメン、食べる？ means the same.

title: も
summary: も means "too" or "also", in place of は, が or を: これも, this too.
parts: ラーメンも食べたい。
I want ramen too.
これも！
This one too!
more: After a question word, with a negative, も means "no…": 何も言わない, says nothing; 誰もいない, nobody's there.

title: です / ます / か
summary: Staff, strangers and bosses speak politely: verbs end in ます, and "is" is です. か on the end makes it a question: やりますか, will you?
parts: バイト、やりますか？
Would you like the job?
ます goes on a verb's stem, the same stem as たい: 食べます, 飲みます.
か at the end of a polite sentence makes it a question. With friends, a rising voice is enough: やる？
今日から、お願いします。
Starting today, please.
more: You'll hear polite speech long before you need to say it. か on a plain sentence can sound blunt, so it mostly goes with です and ます.
Friends would say the plain form instead. Using ます with friends sounds distant; leaving it off with strangers sounds rude.

title: から / まで
summary: から marks where or when something starts; まで, where or when it ends: 朝まで, until morning.
parts: 朝までゲーム。
Games until morning.
They work with places and times, together or apart.

title: と
summary: と joins nouns, "A and B", or marks who you do something with: 店長と, with the manager.
parts: ユキと、コーヒーを飲んだ。
I had coffee with Yuki.
In a list, と goes between each one: これとこれ, this and this.
more: It joins whole lists, unlike や, which only gives examples. For "together", 一緒に often comes after it: ユキと一緒に.

title: ～て / ～てください
summary: A verb's て form plus ください politely asks someone to do something. Friends just use the て form, which also links actions: do this, and then that.
parts: ちょっと待ってください！
Just a moment, please!
て changes a verb just as た does: 待つ, 待った, 待って; 飲む, 飲んだ, 飲んで. With friends, 待って on its own is enough.
ラーメンを食べて、ビールを飲む。
I eat ramen and drink a beer.
In the middle of a sentence, the て form means "and then": one action, then the next.
more: How the て form is made depends on the verb's last sound. る verbs drop る: 食べて. Otherwise う, つ and る become って (買って, 待って, わかって); む, ぶ and ぬ become んで (飲んで, 呼んで, 死んで); く becomes いて (書いて), ぐ becomes いで; す becomes して (話して). 行く is the odd one: 行って. する is して, 来る is 来て.
Adjectives link the same way. An i-adjective swaps its い for くて: 熱くて、うまい, hot and good. Words like きれい and 静か take で: 静かで、優しい, quiet and gentle.

title: に
summary: に marks where something goes, or where it is: 店に来た, came to the shop.
parts: マンガの店に来た。
I came to the manga shop.
It also marks times: 朝に, in the morning. In casual talk it's sometimes dropped after places.

title: ～てる / ～ている
summary: A verb's て form plus いる says something is going on now. Friends shorten ている to てる.
parts: 雨、降ってるよ！
It's raining!
It can also mean a state that's ongoing: 知ってる, I know (I'm in the state of having learned it).
more: With まだ and a negative it means "not yet": まだ食べていない, I haven't eaten yet. A bare 食べない would mean "I don't eat" or "I won't".

title: で
summary: で marks where something happens: 公園で食べた, ate in the park. に is where something is or goes; で is where it's done.
parts: ユキと、公園でミホさんを待つ。
Yuki and I are waiting for Miho in the park.
Compare に: 公園に行く is going to the park; 公園で食べる is eating there.
more: で also marks how something's done (電車で, by train), a cause (雪で, because of the snow), and who's in it (みんなで, all together; 一人で, on your own).

title: から
summary: から after a reason means "because", and what follows is what happens: 寒いから, because it's cold.
parts: 寒いから、ラーメンがうまい。
It's cold, so ramen tastes great.
It's the same から as "from": the reason is where the rest comes from. It can end a sentence too: ベースだから。, because I play bass.

title: ～んだ / ～の？
summary: ん or の before だ or です explains: 帰ったんだ, (the thing is,) he went home. A bare の with a rise asks for the story: 来たの？, you came?
parts: カナダに帰ったんだ。
He went home to Canada.
A bare 帰った just reports. 帰ったんだ gives the story behind it, here why Alex's room is empty. With です it's ～んです.
どこから来たの？
Where did you come from?
A の at the end, said with a rise, is how friends ask when they want to know more. Said flat, it explains, like ～んだ.
more: そうなんだ。
Oh, I see. (So that's how it is.)
After a noun or a na-adjective, な comes first: そうなんだ, 好きなの？
Use it when there's something to explain or react to. On every sentence it sounds pushy, and ～んですか can sound like a challenge: 本当に行くんですか？, are you really going?

title: あのー / えーと
summary: あのー and えーと fill a pause while you think. あのー also gets someone's attention, politely.
parts: えーと…わからないです。
Um… I don't know.
えーと is thinking out loud: you're looking for the answer. あのー is a little shy: you're about to ask or say something.
あのー、ラーメン、食べたいです。
Um, I'd like to eat ramen.

title: ～じゃない / じゃん
summary: じゃない after a noun or na-adjective is the plain "isn't": ベースじゃない, it's not the bass. Said with a rise, it asks "isn't it?", and じゃん says "see?".
parts: ケンタさんじゃない。
It's not Kenta.
じゃない is the negative of だ, the way ～ない is the negative of a verb. With です it's じゃないです.
ユキさんの声じゃない？
Isn't that Yuki's voice?
With a rise, じゃない？ asks the listener to agree. じゃん, short for it, says the same thing as a fact: you should see it too.
いい歌じゃん。
That's a good song, you know.

title: ～けど / ～が
summary: けど after a full sentence means "but": 大きいけど, it's big, but…. が after a sentence means the same, a little more formally.
parts: 行きたくないけど、行きます。
I don't want to go, but I'm going.
けど joins two sentences that pull different ways. Friends say けど; だけど after a noun.
大学は大きいですが、友達がいないです。
The university's big, but I don't have any friends.
が for "but" comes after です or ます more often than after the plain form. At the end of a sentence, けど leaves the rest unsaid, which softens it.

title: ～よう / ～おう
summary: The volitional form is a casual "let's": 行こう, let's go. Said about yourself, it's what you've decided: 歌おう, I'll sing.
parts: みんなで行こう！
Let's all go!
う verbs change their last sound to the お row and add う: 行く, 行こう; 歌う, 歌おう. る verbs swap る for よう: 食べる, 食べよう.
一緒に歌おう！
Let's sing together!
する and 来る have their own: しよう, 来よう. Among friends it's how you suggest anything; ～ましょう is the polite version.

title: ～と思う / ～と
summary: と思う after a plain sentence says what you think: 歌うと思う, I think I'll sing. The same と quotes what someone said: 「来年は歌う」と言った.
parts: 次は歌うと思う。
I think I'll sing next time.
What you think comes first, in the plain form, then と思う. With strangers it's と思います.
ユキの歌は、いいと思う。
I think Yuki's songs are good.
と also marks the words of a quote, before 言う and verbs like it. The quote can be the exact words, in 「」, or put in your own.
ユキは「来年は歌う」と言った。
Yuki said, "I'll sing next year."
more: A noun or na-adjective keeps its だ before と思う: 雨だと思う, I think it's rain.

title: ～って / ～という
summary: って is a casual と言う: 歌うって, says she's singing. という names something: 『雪』という曲, a song called "Snow".
parts: ユキが歌うって？
Yuki's singing, you say?
って quotes what someone said or wrote, and the verb after it often drops: 歌うって (言った). Said with a rise, it checks what you heard.
僕が『ユキさんが歌う』って書いた。
I wrote that Yuki's singing.
という (と plus 言う) puts a name or a description in front of a noun: what it's called.
『雪』という曲です。
It's a song called "Snow".

title: かな / かも
summary: かな at the end of a sentence wonders out loud: 大丈夫かな, will it be okay, I wonder. かも (かもしれない) says it might be so: 出ないかも, it might not come out.
parts: 私、大丈夫かな。
Will I be okay, I wonder.
かな is か (a question) and な (to yourself): a question you don't expect anyone to answer. It's casual.
声が出ないかも。
My voice might not come out.
かも is short for かもしれない, "it might be", about half sure. It goes after the plain form, or straight after a noun: 無理かも, maybe not.

title: ～ましょう / ～ませんか
summary: ～ましょう is the polite "let's": 行きましょう, let's go. ～ませんか invites: 飲みませんか, won't you have some? ～ましょうか offers or suggests: shall we?
parts: 一緒に頑張りましょう。
Let's do our best together.
ましょう goes on the same stem as ます. It's how people at work, staff and strangers suggest doing something together.
コーヒー、飲みませんか？
Would you like some coffee?
～ませんか is a negative question, "won't you…?", which makes it a soft invitation: it leaves room to say no.
more: じゃあ、帰りましょうか。
Well, shall we head home?
With か on the end, ～ましょうか asks: shall we, or shall I? Among friends the casual volitional (行こう) does the same job.

title: ～てもいい / ～てはいけない
summary: A verb's て form plus もいい gives or asks permission: 飲んでもいい, it's okay to drink. Plus はいけない, it forbids: 触ってはいけない, you mustn't touch.
parts: ここで、コーヒーを飲んでもいいですか？
May I drink coffee here?
てもいい is "even if you do, it's fine". As a question, ～てもいいですか asks "may I?", and the answer is often just いいですよ. Friends say ～てもいい？
これは、触ってはいけません。
You mustn't touch this.
てはいけない is "if you do, it won't do": it isn't allowed. Politely it's ～てはいけません.
more: Friends shorten ては to ちゃ and say だめ: 触っちゃだめ, don't touch.

title: ～ないで / ～ないでください
summary: A verb's ない form plus で asks someone not to do it: 撮らないでください, please don't take pictures. In the middle of a sentence it means "without": 食べないで来た, came without eating.
parts: 写真を撮らないでください。
Please don't take pictures.
ないでください is the negative of ～てください: 撮ってください, please take one; 撮らないでください, please don't. Friends drop ください: 撮らないで！
朝、食べないで会社に来ました。
I came to work without eating this morning.
In the middle of a sentence, ～ないで says how the next thing was done: without doing this one, or instead of it.

title: ～える / ～られる
summary: The potential form says what you can do: 歌う (sing), 歌える (can sing); 出る (go out, take part), 出られる (can take part).
parts: 新しいバンドも、出られる？
Can new bands play too?
う verbs change their last sound to the え row and add る: 行く, 行ける; 歌う, 歌える. る verbs take られる: 出る, 出られる. In speech that's often just れる: 出れる.
ユキさん、歌えるじゃん！
Yuki, you can sing!
The new verb changes like a る verb: 行けない (can't go), 歌えた (could sing). 来る becomes 来られる (in speech, often 来れる), and する becomes できる, which you know already.
明日は行けない。
I can't go tomorrow.

title: ～たら
summary: ら on a verb's past form says "if" or "when": 勝ったら, if we win. It's the everyday way to say "if".
parts: もし勝ったら、どうする？
What do we do if we win?
Take the plain past and add ら, then say what happens. もし (if) in front is optional; it flags early that an "if" is coming.
雨が降ったら、どうする？
What if it rains?
負けたら、また来年。
If we lose, there's next year.
more: For something sure to happen, たら means "when" or "once": 終わったら, when it's over.
練習が終わったら、ラーメン食べよう。
Let's have ramen once practice is over.

title: ～なきゃ / ～なくてもいい
summary: なきゃいけない or なくちゃ on a verb's ない stem says you have to: 練習しなくちゃ, I have to practise. なくてもいい says you don't: 緊張しなくてもいい, no need to be nervous.
parts: 練習しなくちゃ。
I have to practise.
Take the ない form and swap ない for なくちゃ: 練習しない, 練習しなくちゃ. It's short for なくては (いけない): "if I don't, it won't do".
動画を送らなきゃいけない。
We have to send a video.
新しい曲じゃなくてもいい。
It doesn't have to be a new song.
なくてもいい is the other way round: even not doing it is fine. After a noun it's じゃなくてもいい.
more: なきゃ is short for なければ, "if not", and does the same job. Friends often drop the いけない. In writing and formal talk it's the whole なければならない.

title: ～くなる / ～になる / ～く
summary: なる means become: 暑くなる, get hot; 上手になる, get good. An adjective's く form on its own says how something's done: 早く起きる, get up early.
parts: 夏が、暑くなった。
Summer has got hot.
歌が、上手になった。
Your singing's got good.
An i-adjective swaps い for く before なる. A noun or na-adjective takes に.
今は、うまく歌える。
Now I can sing it well.
The same く form, with no なる after it, tells how something's done: 早く (early, fast), 楽しく (happily), うまく (well).
more: Loud isn't 大きく but 大きい声で: 大きい声で歌う, sing loud.

title: ～みたい / ～そう
summary: みたい after a noun or a plain verb says it seems so: 雨みたい, sounds like rain. そう on an adjective's stem says how it looks: 怖そう, she looks scary.
parts: 雨みたい。
Sounds like rain.
みたい is a guess from what you see or hear. It goes straight after a noun, or after the plain form of a verb or adjective: 怒ってるみたい, she seems angry.
リン、怒ってるみたい。
Rin seems angry.
リンさん、ちょっと怖そう。
Rin looks a bit scary.
そう goes on an adjective with its い dropped (怖い, 怖そう; 楽しい, 楽しそう) or on a verb's stem. It's how something looks to you, before you know. いい becomes よさそう.
more: Before a noun it's みたいな: 雨みたいな曲, a song like rain. In writing and formal talk it's ～ようだ.
On a verb, そう often means "about to": 泣きそう, about to cry; 降りそう, looks like rain.

title: ～ちゃう / ～てしまう
summary: しまう after a verb's て form says it's done and over, often when you didn't want it: 切れてしまった, it went and snapped. Friends say ちゃう: 切れちゃった.
parts: 切れちゃった。
It snapped.
て plus しまう shrinks to ちゃう, and で plus しまう to じゃう: 忘れちゃう, 飲んじゃう. In the past, ちゃった and じゃった.
歌、忘れちゃった。
I forgot the song.
It's often a small "oops": it happened, and it can't be undone. It can also just say something's done completely, or can't be helped.
私、緊張しちゃう。
I can't help getting nervous.
more: The full てしまう is for writing and polite talk: 切れてしまいました.

title: ～てみる
summary: みる after a verb's て form means do it and see how it goes: 歌ってみる, try singing it.
parts: 歌ってみて。
Try singing it.
It's the verb 見る (see), written in kana: do something, and see what happens.
言葉、書いてみた。
I tried writing the words.
みる changes like 見る: やってみた (I tried it), やってみよう (let's give it a go), 静かにしてみて (try it quieter).
もう一回、やってみよう。
Let's try it once more.

title: だけ / しか
summary: だけ after a word means only that: 三曲だけ, just three songs. しか with a negative verb means the same, with a feeling of not enough: 三曲しかない, we've only got three songs.
parts: 三曲しかない。
We've only got three songs.
しか always comes with a negative: しかない (there's only), しか知らない (only know). It says there should be more.
三曲だけ。
Just three songs.
だけ just says that's all there is, with no complaint, and works with any verb: 一回だけ (only once), 俺だけ (only me).
ステージは、一回だけ。
We only get one go on the stage.
more: それだけ, "that's all", ends what you have to say.

title: ～に行く / へ
summary: に after a verb's stem says what you're going or coming for: 見に行く, go to see; 見せに来た, came to show. へ marks where you're headed, much like に: スタジオへ行く.
parts: ラーメンを食べに行こう。
Let's go and get ramen.
Take a verb's ます stem (食べます, 食べ), add に, then a verb of going: 行く, 来る or 帰る. The に says what the trip is for.
ユキに見せに来た。
I came to show Yuki.
スタジオへ行った。
I went to the studio.
へ is the kana he, but read え. It points toward a place, and with 行く and 来る it does the same job as に.
more: A する verb's stem is し: 練習しに行く, go to practise. 何しに来たの？ asks what someone came for.

title: より / ～のほうが
summary: より marks what you compare against: 私の絵より, than my drawing. のほうが picks the side that's more so: プロのほうが上手, the pro's better.
parts: プロの絵は、私の絵よりきれい。
The pro's drawing is cleaner than mine.
A は B より, then an adjective: A is more so than B. There's no word for "more"; the adjective does the work.
プロのほうが、上手。
The pro's better.
ほう means side. A noun takes の before it (プロのほう), a verb doesn't (勝つほう). が marks it as the one that's more so.
春より、上手になった。
I've got better since spring.
more: To ask which of two, say どっち: どっちがいい？, which is better? The answer often has のほうが, and sometimes より too.
For "the most", put 一番 (number one) before the adjective: 一番好き, like it best; 一番大事, the most important.

title: ～とき
summary: とき after a verb, an adjective, or a noun with の says when something happens: 行くとき, when I go; 子供のとき, when I was a kid.
parts: 仕事に行くとき、いつも歌を聞く。
When I go to work, I always listen to music.
とき (時) is the word for time. What comes before it says which time: a plain verb, an adjective (忙しいとき, when I'm busy), a na-adjective with な (静かなとき), or a noun with の.
子供のとき、毎日マンガを読んでいた。
When I was a kid, I read manga every day.
A past verb before とき says it had already happened: 見たとき, when I saw it. A present verb says it hadn't yet, or happens every time.
ユキのバンドを見たとき、すごいと思った。
When I saw Yuki's band, I thought it was amazing.
more: Compare たら: 見たら leans toward "once I see it" or "if"; 見たとき just says at the time.

title: ～前に / ～た後で / ～てから
summary: 前に after a plain verb says before: 寝る前に, before bed. 後で after a past verb says after: 終わった後で, after it's over. から after a verb's て form says after, and then: 食べてから, after eating.
parts: 仕事に行く前に、コーヒーを飲む。
Before I go to work, I have a coffee.
The verb before 前に is always plain present, even in a story told in the past: 寝る前に読んだ, I read before bed.
仕事が終わった後で、ラーメンを食べる。
After work's over, I have ramen.
後で (あとで) goes the other way: the verb before it is always past. On its own, 後で means "later".
食べてから、行こう。
Let's eat first, then go.
more: ～てから puts two things in order: this one, and only then that one. It's the everyday way to say one thing has to come first.

title: や / ～たり / など
summary: や lists a few nouns out of more: ラーメンや卵, ramen, eggs and so on. ～たり does the same for things you do: 読んだり、書いたり. など after a list says it goes on.
parts: 休みの日は、マンガを読んだり、ゲームをしたりする。
On my days off I read manga, play games, that kind of thing.
Take a verb's past form (読んだ, した) and add り: 読んだり, したり. Give two or so, then する in whatever form the sentence needs: したりする, したりした. In casual talk the last する often drops: 読んだり、書いたり。
コンビニで、ビールや水を買った。
I bought beer, water and stuff at the konbini.
や joins nouns like と does, but と gives the whole list, and や only a few of them. ビールと水 is just those two; ビールや水 is those and more.
more: マンガやゲームなどが好き。
I like manga, games, that sort of thing.
など after the last one says there's more where that came from. It often closes a list made with や, and can follow just one: ラーメンなど, ramen and the like.
Friends often say とか for both: ラーメンとか、卵とか.

title: ～の
summary: の after a verb or adjective makes it something you can talk about like a noun: 歌うのが好き, I like singing; 大きいのを買った, I bought the big one.
parts: ユキが歌うのが、好き。
I love it when Yuki sings.
A plain verb, then の, and the whole thing works like a noun: it takes が, を, は or も after it. 一人で食べるのは、寂しい: eating alone is lonely.
ユキが歌うのを、聞いた。
I heard Yuki sing.
大きいのを買った。
I bought the big one.
After an adjective, の stands for a thing you've already talked about: 大きいの, the big one; 新しいの, the new one. A na-adjective takes な first: 静かなの, the quiet one.
more: With 見る and 聞く, the の is what you see or hear going on: 笑うのを見た, I saw her laugh.

title: ～てくれる / ～てあげる / ～てもらう
summary: After a verb's て form, くれる, あげる and もらう say who a favour is for: 作ってくれた, someone made it for me; 作ってあげた, I made it for someone; 作ってもらった, I had someone make it.
parts: ソラが、コーヒーを入れてくれた。
Sora made me a coffee.
私が、ソラにコーヒーを入れてあげた。
I made Sora a coffee.
～てくれる: someone does something for me, or my side, with a little thanks. ～てあげる goes the other way: I do something for someone else.
ケンタに、写真を撮ってもらった。
I got Kenta to take a photo.
～てもらう looks at the same favour from my side: I get it done. The one who does it takes に.
more: Said to the person's face, ～てあげる can sound like a big favour, so people often say just 入れるよ instead.
To ask for a favour: 撮ってもらってもいい？, could you take it for me?

title: ～ので / ～し
summary: ので gives a reason, softer than から: 仕事なので, since I've got work. し adds a reason, hinting there are more: 安いし、うまいし, it's cheap, it's good.
parts: 明日は仕事なので、もう寝る。
I've got work tomorrow, so I'm off to bed.

ので goes after a plain verb or adjective: 雨が降っているので, 寒いので. A noun or na-adjective takes な first: 仕事なので, 静かなので. It sounds softer and a little more formal than から, so it suits polite explanations and apologies: 仕事があるので、行けません。
店長のラーメンは、安いし、うまいし、最高。
The manager's ramen is cheap, it's good, it's the best.
し after a plain form lists a reason, and leaves room for more. Two in a row make a case for something.
寒いし、もう帰ろう。
It's cold and all, so let's head home.
more: Among friends, から is the usual one.
Just one し says "for one thing": the rest go unsaid.

title: ～のに
summary: のに joins two things where the second isn't what you'd expect: 練習したのに、うまくできなかった, I practised, and still it didn't go well.
parts: 練習したのに、うまく歌えなかった。
Even though I practised, I couldn't sing it well.
のに goes after a plain verb or adjective. A noun or na-adjective takes な first: 休みなのに, even though it's a day off. It carries a feeling: surprise, disappointment, sometimes a complaint.
休みなのに、仕事に行った。
I went to work even though it was my day off.
見たかったのに。
And I wanted to see it, too.
At the end of a sentence, のに is a sigh about what should have been, with the rest left unsaid.
more: Compare けど: けど just says "but"; のに says it went against what should have happened. Unlike けど, のに can't lead into a request, a suggestion or a plan: not 雨なのに、行こう, but 雨だけど、行こう.

title: ～ほうがいい / ～すぎる
summary: ほうがいい gives advice: 寝たほうがいい, you'd better get some sleep. すぎる after a stem says too much: 飲みすぎた, I drank too much.
parts: 今日は、寝たほうがいいよ。
You'd better get some sleep today.
For doing something, the verb before ほうがいい is usually past: 行ったほうがいい, you should go. For not doing it, use ない: 行かないほうがいい, better not go. It's the ほう of のほうが: of the two ways, this one's better.
夜、ビールを飲みすぎた。
I drank too much beer last night.
すぎる goes on a verb's stem (飲み, 食べ, し) or an adjective without its い (高い, 高すぎる; 静か, 静かすぎる), and changes like 食べる: すぎた, すぎない.
このラーメン、熱すぎる。
This ramen's too hot.
more: The stem すぎ works as a noun on its own: 飲みすぎ, too much drinking; 練習しすぎ, too much practice.

title: ～たことがある
summary: A past verb, then ことがある, says it's happened at least once: 行ったことがある, I've been there. ことがない says never.
parts: カナダに行ったことがある？
Have you ever been to Canada?
こと is a thing, an event: 行ったこと, the having gone. ある says there's such a thing in your past. Ask with ある？, and answer ある or ない.
ステージで歌ったことがない。
I've never sung on a stage.
ない says never. は or も can take the place of が: 見たことはある, I've seen it, at least; 食べたこともない, I've never even eaten it.
マンガは、読んだことはある。
Manga, I've read.
more: It's about what you've been through, not about today: ラーメンを食べた is what you just did; ラーメンを食べたことがある says you know what it's like.
